scenes.tts: Draw a soft brush across the hairy skin of a human forearm. Go slowly, then faster. One class of slow nerve fibre changes how hard it fires. Ask people to rate the same strokes, and they call the middle speeds the most pleasant. Is that why a slow stroke can feel nice?
scenes.visual: forearm skin with hairs; brush sweeps at changing speed; one fibre under the skin sends spikes whose rate changes; question mark appears
scenes.narration: Draw a soft brush across the hairy skin of a human forearm. Go slowly, then faster. One class of slow nerve fibre changes how hard it fires. Ask people to rate the same strokes, and they call the middle speeds the most pleasant. Is that why a slow stroke can feel nice?

scenes.tts: The fibre is called a C tactile afferent, or C T afferent. It is a touch fibre with an unmyelinated axon, so it has no insulating wrap. It is the human counterpart of what mouse papers call a C L T M R. Whether the two names mean the same cells is a question we return to. To listen to one fibre, researchers use microneurography. A fine electrode goes through the skin into a nerve. It records single axons in an awake person.
scenes.visual: labelled CT ending and axon, electrode through skin into nerve, single-axon trace appears

scenes.tts: Loken and colleagues treated stroke velocity as a stimulus feature, like orientation or frequency. They brushed the forearm at a range of controlled velocities. They recorded single C T afferents in healthy volunteers. Firing traced an inverted U. It was highest for strokes between about one and ten centimetres per second.

scenes.tts: Now a second experiment. In separate sessions, a separate group of volunteers rated how pleasant the same strokes felt. Their ratings traced the same inverted U. But the two curves came from different people.
scenes.visual: second panel: different group of people icons, ratings curve of same shape in a different colour; labels recorded group and rating group

scenes.tts: Think of two thermometers in different rooms. Both read highest at noon. They agree, but neither shows that one causes the other. The same is true here. The result is a correspondence. It does not show that C T firing is needed for pleasantness. A later study adds a limit. It reported nineteen patients tested before and after a cut to the anterolateral spinal cord. Brush pleasantness ratings did not significantly change. That rules out one obligatory route. It does not say which route carries the signal instead.

scenes.tts: There is one more reason for care. In mouse hairy skin, at least three afferent populations are candidates for detecting a stroke. They are not the same cells. So gentle stroking is not a job for C fibres alone. Keep the rule. Two matching curves are a correspondence. They do not show which fibre is needed.
